blocks.v: The Fence
“It’s a good fence,” Vex said.
“That isn’t helpful,” Owen said.
“I’m complimenting it. Somebody put it up in four hours and it’s better than anything the county has built since I was born.” She ran two fingers down a post. “Which is why we’re not climbing it.”
“You said we were climbing it.”

“I said we were going in. You added the climbing part.” Vex started walking north along the fence line with her hands in her jacket pockets. “You climb a fence when you don’t know the property, and I know this property.”

The dumpster pad was around the corner, a concrete rectangle with two dumpsters on it and a smell that had outlived the school by six months. The fence came right up to the edge of the pad and stopped.
“Owen, that site plan you found. Did it say where the fence goes?”
“It pointed at a county drawing. Property line.”

“You’re kidding me,” Owen said.
“I’m not. Pip goes first, because Pip doesn’t care about her shoulders.”
Pip went through sideways without touching either side. Vex went second and made it look easy, which it wasn’t. Owen went third and made a noise he refused to discuss.

The hatch was two steel doors set flat in the ground with a chain and a padlock across them. Vex didn’t bother with the lock. She got a flathead under the hasp and lifted the whole thing out of the concrete, because the concrete had been poured badly in 2011 and nobody ever came back to fix it.
“Ninety seconds,” she said. “Anybody want to say something nice to me?”
“Later,” Owen said.
“With you that’s the same as no.”

blocks.v: The Wardrobe Room
The basement hall smelled like floor wax and old paper. Two flashlights made two circles on the tile, and Pip didn’t use one, which stopped being unsettling around the third week you knew her.
Forty feet down on the left there was a door with a bad hinge, and behind it a short flight of concrete steps, and at the bottom of those, the wardrobe room.

It was bigger than Owen expected and a lot fuller. Thirteen steamer trunks along the back wall, numbered in white paint by a shop teacher who retired in 1991. A rack of choir robes on a pipe. Boxes of hats. A shelf of shoes lined up in pairs with every toe pointed the same direction, which Owen decided immediately was the worst thing in the room.
Trunk seven stood open with nothing in it but a folded sheet of tissue paper.
Vex put her light down in the corner, on a scuff pattern in the dust. Four sets of bare footprints headed out, and none of them came back.
Pip wasn’t looking at any of it. She stood in the middle of the room with her head tilted at the near wall, where a typed inventory sheet hung in a plastic sleeve on a nail.
“I need everybody quiet for a minute.”
“You can just read it,” Owen said. “It’s four feet away.”
“I know. I am not reading it yet. There is a hum in the north wall and I want to hear it before I know anything, because once I know something I stop hearing properly.”
“That isn’t how ears work.”

blocks.v: “It is how mine work.”
They waited. The building settled somewhere above them and three hundred yards away a generator ran.
“It is here,” Pip said. “Not in the wires. In the room, behind the trunks.” She turned her head about an inch. “It is not talking. It is only on.”
“Is it listening to us?”

“It is always listening, and that is not the same as caring.” She stepped to the wall and took the whole page in at once, the way she does. “Two hundred and six items. Last touched by hand in November of 2014, in pencil, by somebody with a bad grip. Trunk seven is items one sixty through one seventy-four. Spring production wardrobe, assorted.”
“Read me seven.”

“One grey hooded sweatshirt, adult large. One pair of boxing gloves, vinyl, prop only, not for use. One practice bow, string missing, with twelve blunt arrows in a canvas quiver. One knitted green cap, ears sewn on. One suit of plate armor and sword, stage construction, painted canvas over a wooden frame, damage to the right shoulder noted. One orange dress, printed, child large. One pointed hat, felt, tip bent. One straw hat. One pair of rubber boots.”
Nobody said anything for a second.
Owen got there first. “Say the armor again.”
“Painted canvas over a wooden frame.”
“Pip, that thing stopped a delivery truck this week.” Vex had turned all the way around. “Tovar put his shoulder into it and it didn’t rock. That’s steel or I’ve never touched steel in my life.”
“Yes.”

blocks.v: “So the sheet’s wrong.”

“The sheet is correct. The sheet describes what was supposed to be in that trunk, and until Tuesday night that is exactly what was in it.” Pip turned around to face them. “It did not copy the costume. It read what the costume was for.”
Owen sat down on the edge of a trunk, which he never does.
“Say that again in a way I can write down.”

“A program says knight. An inventory says the knight is made of painted canvas. Those two documents disagree with each other, so it fixed the one that was broken.” Her voice didn’t change, because it doesn’t. “It made a real knight, correct in every detail, and it left the dent in the shoulder, because somebody had written the dent down too.”
“The bow was missing a string,” Vex said slowly.
“It is not missing a string now.”
“And the gloves say prop only. Not for use.”
“Rocco’s gloves are leather.”
Nobody had anything to say to that, and all three of them noticed at the same time that Felix wasn’t there.
“Okay,” Owen said. “So it read a shelf full of pretend things and it made four of them true.”
“It read the only four protectors this town ever bothered to write down.” Pip looked back at the sheet. “I told it we were frightened, and that is what it had to work with.”
Vex looked into the bottom of trunk seven, at the straw hat lying there next to a pair of rubber boots.
“We got lucky,” she said.

blocks.v: Ten Feet Apart
Across town, the Warehouse was doing a bad job of waiting.

Milo had checked his phone eleven times in forty minutes, which for him is pacing a hole in the rug. Lena had three edits open and hadn’t made a cut in twenty-five. Felix had built two things and taken one of them back apart.
Then Felix said, “Guys. How long has that been going on?”

Up on the high shelf, Monke was sitting straight up with a granola bar in one hand and no interest in eating it. Ten feet away, on top of the router, the dragon was sitting up too, plates up along its back, tail hanging straight down.
They were looking right at each other.
“I think it’s a contest,” Felix whispered. He got his phone out. “I’ve got five bucks on the monkey.”
“You don’t have five bucks,” Lena said.
“I have a gift card to a store that closed.”
Four minutes later he said it was boring and went back to his bench.

Twenty minutes after that, Lena looked up because the fan clicked, and neither animal had moved so much as an inch. When Owen’s text finally came in at ten to one, they were both asleep, and they’d fallen asleep at the same second. Nobody in that room ever found out who won, and Felix told people for the rest of his life that it was the monkey.

blocks.v: Old Bell Road
At ten past six the next morning, Private Kyle Dunphy had the Old Bell Road stop with Sergeant Marisol Reyes forty yards back and a jaw that still ached from Thursday.
Dame Ottilie was standing in the road again.

Reyes had written it up twice already. Her report said, in the plainest language she could manage, that the obstruction could not be moved, arrested or shocked, that it had never threatened anybody, and that it had twice offered to hold somebody’s coffee. She recommended moving the checkpoint a hundred yards north, where there was no obstruction, since the obstruction never followed anybody anywhere.
Lieutenant Pace read the report. He also had two new squads, a specialist team, and a note from an admiral in the admiral’s own handwriting, so he ordered the checkpoint held.
At fourteen past, Ray Toomey came around the bend in a five-ton delivery truck doing forty.

Ray had run that route for nineteen years and had been up since four. He saw a person standing in his road and did what anybody would do, which was stand on the brakes, and then the back end started coming around on him, and then he aimed for the shoulder, where Private Kyle Dunphy was standing with a clipboard.
Ottie got between them. She set her feet and put a shoulder out, and a five-ton truck hit a suit of steel plate with a girl inside it.

blocks.v: The truck lost, and that was the part nobody in Millbrook ever got over.

The front end folded up like a soda can and the whole thing stopped eleven feet earlier than it had any business stopping. Ottie slid backward maybe four inches. The airbag went off, and Ray sat there in a cloud of talcum powder with both hands still on the wheel.
Ottie turned around. “Sir, are you hurt?”
Ray Toomey said a word.
“That’s all right. I’m sorry about your truck. I don’t know how to pay for a truck, because nobody’s explained money to me yet.”
Dunphy had sat down on the shoulder without deciding to. Reyes got to him in nine seconds and crouched down.
“Look at me. You’re on the ground, but you’re fine.”
“She got in front of it.”
“She did.”
“Sergeant, she got in front of a truck for me, and I’ve been pointing a checkpoint at her for two days. That’s the worst I’ve ever felt about anything.”
“Then write it down exactly the way you said it,” Reyes said. “It’s going in my report and I want it in yours too.”

She stood up and took stock. A folded-up delivery truck. A girl in armor apologizing to a man in an airbag. And eleven civilians on the far shoulder with their phones up, at six in the morning, on a road that officially had nobody on it, guarded by a unit that was officially in a soybean field in Georgia.
“They’re going to hate this,” Reyes said, to nobody at all.

blocks.v: Four In The Warehouse
They ended up at the Warehouse, because there was nowhere else to put them and because Vex went and got them.
It was the strangest afternoon in the building’s history, and that building has housed a crocodile.

Ottie couldn’t get the right shoulder plate off, because the truck had seized the strapping behind it and bent something under the dent. Felix went at it for two hours with tin snips, a rubber mallet and a hair dryer, talking the entire time, while Ottie sat perfectly still on a milk crate and answered every question he asked her.
“Does that pinch?”
“Yes.”
“Bad pinch or regular pinch?”
“I have nothing to compare it to. This is my fourth day.”
“Right. Sorry. Okay, hold still, because this either works or it sets your hair on fire.”
“I don’t believe I have hair.”
“Then we’ll find out together.”
Rocco found the fighting game and was terrible at it, and he apologized to the television twice. Owen tried to explain the controller, and Rocco held it like a bird.
“You press this one to punch.”
“I press a button and the man punches.”
“Yes.”

blocks.v: “Why?”
“Because it’s a game.”
“But he’s not doing it. I’m doing it, and he doesn’t know he’s punching.” Rocco looked honestly troubled. “Does he mind?”
Owen opened his mouth, closed it, went back to his desk and didn’t speak for eleven minutes.

Wren spent the afternoon on the roof, because she liked being able to see the whole street at once, and she came down only to report things. A gray car had gone around the block three times. Two soldiers were buying pie. Aunt Carol was coming up Crescent with a casserole and would arrive in four minutes. She was right every time, and she said all of it in the same soft apologetic voice, and by dinner Vex was calling her the weather.
Sybil sat down next to Lena, looked at the laptop and said, “That’s an awful lot of light for such a small box.”
“It’s a computer.”
“Mm.” Sybil watched the timeline scrub past for a while, and then she reached over and put one finger on the trackpad, and every device in the building shut off at the same moment.
“Oh,” Sybil said. “Sorry, dear. It does that near me sometimes.”
Owen made a noise like a kettle.
“Everything saved,” Pip said. “I checked on the way down.”
“You checked on the way down.”
“I am fast.”

blocks.v: Around six, Milo came out of the back and stood in the doorway and looked at all of it. A boxer losing a video game with tremendous dignity. An archer on the roof. A witch apologizing to a router. A knight with a stuck shoulder plate getting worked on by a kid with a hair dryer, with the pig asleep against her leg like she was a radiator.
“How much trouble are we in?” Lena said.

“Eleven people filmed a truck lose a fight with a suit of armor, so a lot.” He drank his coffee. “And Crane is going to want a curfew he can actually enforce, and he can’t have one, because the curfew belongs to the dumbest man in this county.”
Lena turned her head. “Say that again.”
Item Forty-One
Late that night Pip sat on the floor of the Shop, watching Felix sleep at his bench with his face on his arms and the mallet still in his hand.
Vex sat down next to her.
“You’ve been weird since the basement.”
“Two hundred and six items,” Pip said. “I counted two hundred and five.”
Vex waited, because Pip doesn’t do dramatic pauses. She does processing pauses, and they look the same and last longer.
“Item forty-one. Nineteen sixty-eight. A child’s coat, black wool, three orange buttons, size six.”

“None of them. There is a note beside it in pencil, from 2014, in the same bad handwriting as the rest of the sheet.” Pip looked up. “It says not returned.”
